messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For most of his career, Minh Tran had been the one people called in crisis. At 68, a widowed public defender with a reputation for steadiness, he was used to walking into courthouse holding cells and hearing frightened, angry stories without losing his bearings. That changed after his adult daughter was killed during a home invasion six months ago. He was not there when it happened, but he arrived soon afterward, and what has stayed with him is not a coherent sequence so much as shattered fragments: the front door ajar, a lamp overturned, the sound of a neighbor crying in the hallway, and, most piercingly, a short burst of his daughter’s voice on the 911 recording that police later played for him. In his mind, the memories do not settle into a single account. They come in jagged pieces, and when they do he hears sounds as if they are happening again—the panic in her voice, the banging at the door, the operator asking questions no one could answer in time. Each return of the memory is soaked in overwhelming grief.

In the first weeks after the funeral, Minh tried to manage those intrusions in the practical way he approached everything else. He stopped watching the evening news and turned off legal dramas or crime shows as soon as a break-in or assault appeared. He began eating constantly in the late evenings, telling himself that a full stomach gave him something else to feel besides the hollow drop that came when his daughter’s voice intruded. The more the memory arrived in those broken sensory flashes, the more urgently he looked for ways to block it out. He could not bear anything on television or in the newspaper that resembled what had happened to her, because even a brief story about violence was enough to pull him back into those disconnected moments and the grief they carried.

Those same fragments also left him feeling as if danger were immediate and unfinished. Because he could not hold the event in his mind as something completed, he reacted to ordinary sounds as if they signaled another attack. A knock in his apartment building, footsteps outside his door, voices rising in the street at night could set off a surge of fear before he had even oriented himself. He became preoccupied with locks and windows, checking them repeatedly before bed and again after waking in the night, not because he thought through a specific threat each time but because his body seemed convinced that someone could force their way in at any moment. What frightened him most was how quickly he went from sitting in his armchair to standing breathless in the hallway, certain for a second that something was wrong.

That sense of danger spread into his work. At the courthouse, Minh found himself scanning faces in waiting areas and elevators, vigilant for men who seemed agitated, intoxicated, or unpredictable. He had spent decades around distressed defendants and distraught families, but now he watched people with a strained, suspicious attention that exhausted him. When a client raised his voice in an interview room, Minh felt the old jolt of alarm and afterward checked his office door twice before leaving. Because he felt perpetually on edge, he leaned harder on the habits that seemed to contain it: more checking, more avoidance of media, more eating after work to settle himself. For an hour or two these things dulled the fear, but they also kept his world organized around the possibility of danger, so that every unvetted sound or unfamiliar person seemed to require even more vigilance.

The cycle tightened over the following months. Nights were the worst. After checking the deadbolt, he would lie down, hear a creak in the building, and suddenly the broken pieces of the night of his daughter’s death would flare up again, especially the sounds. He would get back out of bed to inspect the windows, then stand in the kitchen eating cereal or leftover rice straight from the container, trying to push the audio fragments out of his head. By morning he was ashamed of how little control he had, yet the poor sleep and constant alertness made the memories easier to trigger again the next day. Even at work, after reading case files involving assault or burglary, he would avoid related coverage online and leave his office to make another round of checking the door, all while the same clipped sounds replayed internally.

Lately, Minh has started to worry that he is becoming someone his daughter would not recognize: a man who mistrusts strangers, startles at harmless noises, and spends his evenings circling his apartment to make sure it is secure. The change has begun to affect his work; he has shortened client meetings, avoided certain assignments when he can, and once snapped at an investigator who came up behind him unexpectedly in the office. He finally sought help after finding himself frozen at home one night, hand on the lock, hearing his daughter’s voice so vividly that he could not tell for a moment whether it was memory or something happening outside his own door. He says he is afraid that if this continues, he will never again feel that the world is anything but moments away from taking another person he loves, and he hopes, cautiously, that treatment might help him remember his daughter without being dragged back into the sound of losing her.
